guide_description: Three days covering San Sebastian's essential character: the pintxos-dense Old Town on the bay, the Belle Epoque promenade and riverfront of the city center, and the quieter western beaches and hilltop panoramas. Each day is geographically self-contained and walkable.

days.cluster_tagline: The densest concentration of pintxos bars in the world, pinned between a fortress hill and the bay
days.neighborhood_description: San Sebastian's old quarter is a tight grid of narrow streets rebuilt in the early 19th century after a fire. It is bordered by the Monte Urgull promontory to the north, La Concha bay to the west, and the mouth of the Urumea river to the east. Every ground floor seems to be a bar; every bar counter carries a landscape of pintxos.

morning.activity_title: Monte Urgull and Castillo de la Mota
morning.notes: Climb from the Parte Vieja side via the staircase off Plaza de Zuloaga rather than the longer path from the port - it takes about 15 minutes and deposits you directly at the castle battlements. The Cristo de la Mota statue on the summit gives a clear 360-degree view of La Concha bay, the two flanking hills, and the full sweep of the Cantabrian coast. The interior of the castle holds a small free museum on the city's military history.

walk_to_next.to: Basilica de Santa Maria del Coro

afternoon.activity_title: Basilica de Santa Maria del Coro
afternoon.notes: The churrigueresque facade on Calle Mayor is one of the most theatrical baroque frontages in the Basque Country - look for the sculpted anchors and maritime motifs worked into the stonework, a reference to the city's seafaring identity. The interior is cooler and quieter than the street outside, and the painted vaults are easy to miss if you keep your eyes at counter level.

evening.activity_title: Plaza de la Constitucion and pintxos crawl
evening.notes: The numbered balconies on the square's upper floors were originally rented as bullfight viewing boxes when the arena occupied the plaza - the numbers are still painted on. For the pintxos crawl, the standard move is one or two pintxos and a txakoli at each bar rather than a full sitting; Bar Nestor on Calle Pescaderia is famous for its tortilla (only two made per day, reserve a slice when you arrive), and Bar Zeruko on Calle Pescaderia does avant-garde cold pintxos in small glasses.

if_time_permits.notes: A 16th-century Dominican convent expanded with a striking perforated-steel modern wing that blends into Monte Urgull's slope. The permanent collection covers Basque history and ethnography from prehistory to the 20th century; the cloister murals by Jose Maria Sert are enormous and technically impressive. The best rainy-day anchor in the Parte Vieja.

walk_from_main_route.from: Basilica de Santa Maria del Coro

if_time_permits.notes: The covered market on Plaza de Sarriegi has a fish hall on the upper level and a produce hall below - best visited before noon when the anchovy and bonito vendors are still active. The range of preserved and fresh Cantabrian seafood on a single counter is a useful introduction to what drives the local kitchen.

days.cluster_tagline: Belle Epoque promenade, the city's showpiece beach, and the surfer neighbourhood across the river
days.neighborhood_description: The 19th-century grid expansion of San Sebastian wraps the south shore of La Concha bay and steps across the Urumea river into Gros, the younger neighbourhood fronting Zurriola beach. The Paseo de la Concha promenade, the Miramar Palace gardens, and the colonnaded balustrades were all built during the Spanish royal family's summer residency.

morning.notes: Walk the full promenade from the old town end to the Miramar headland rather than turning back - the iron balustrades with their scallop-shell cutouts were designed by Jose Goicoa in the 1880s and are the visual signature of the bay. The floating pontoon platform anchored offshore is the Isla de Santa Clara ferry landing; early morning the beach is used exclusively by local swimmers doing laps parallel to the shore.

afternoon.notes: The Queen Regent Maria Cristina had this English-style country house built in 1893 on the headland separating La Concha from Ondarreta beach. The palace interior is not publicly accessible but the gardens are free and the headland position gives simultaneous views of both bays. The formal rose garden on the lower terrace faces directly onto the open Atlantic.

evening.activity_title: Kursaal Congress Centre and Zurriola Beach
evening.notes: Rafael Moneo's two translucent cubic auditoriums on the Zurriola beachfront are best seen at dusk when the interior lighting glows through the laminated glass panels like two illuminated boulders. The Gros neighbourhood behind the building is where local surfers and young residents eat - the pintxos bars here (Calle de Zabaleta, Calle de General Jauregui) are less touristed and slightly cheaper than the Parte Vieja, with as much quality.

if_time_permits.notes: The small island anchored in the center of La Concha bay runs a seasonal ferry from the port (roughly June to September). The island has a small beach, a lighthouse, and picnic benches with arguably the best angle on the full bay panorama. Tide-dependent - the swimming cove on the south side is only accessible at low tide.

days.cluster_tagline: The western hill with panoramic views, a century-old funicular, and the quiet end of the bay
days.neighborhood_description: The western promontory closing off La Concha bay, accessed via the quiet Ondarreta residential beach. Monte Igueldo was developed in the early 20th century as a leisure hill - funicular, vintage amusement park, and a belvedere tower that gives the definitive view of the full bay arc. The Peine del Viento sculptures at the base of the hill are among the most celebrated public artworks in Spain.

morning.notes: Eduardo Chillida's three rusted steel sculptures are anchored directly into the wave-cut rock platform at the base of Monte Igueldo - arrive at high tide or during a west swell when the sea surges through the blowholes cut into the rocks, shooting jets of water into the air. The surrounding terraced walkway was designed by Luis Pena Ganchegui; the integrated relationship between sculpture, geology, and sea is the point, not just the objects in isolation.

afternoon.activity_title: Funicular de Igueldo and Monte Igueldo summit
afternoon.notes: The funicular has been running since 1912 and the wooden cars are original - the ride up takes about four minutes and the cars pass each other at the midpoint. At the top, walk past the vintage amusement park rides to the stone belvedere tower at the far end of the summit for the unobstructed view: La Concha arc, both flanking hills, the old town grid, and on clear days the French Basque coast east toward Biarritz. The amusement park is low-key and mostly aimed at children, but the roller coaster built into the hillside dates from 1928.

evening.activity_title: Ondarreta Beach and Paseo Eduard Chillida
evening.notes: Ondarreta is the residential beach used by locals who find La Concha too crowded in summer - the western end, closest to Monte Igueldo, stays in shade earlier but catches the last horizontal light on the water. Walk the seafront promenade back toward the city center for the full bay view from ground level, with Monte Urgull visible at the far end and the old town silhouetted against the evening sky.

if_time_permits.notes: Eduardo Chillida's former farmhouse and sculpture garden, reopened in 2019 after a decade-long closure. About 40 large-scale steel and stone works are distributed across 11 hectares of woodland - the experience of finding a two-ton corten steel form in a clearing of oak trees is unlike any conventional sculpture museum. Requires a taxi or bus from the city center (roughly 20 minutes south toward Hernani); plan as a half-day excursion rather than a quick stop.

if_time_permits.activity_title: Real Club de Tenis de San Sebastian
if_time_permits.notes: The 1909 club building fronting Ondarreta beach is a fine example of the Belle Epoque resort architecture that defined the city during the royal summer-residency era. Worth a look from the promenade as a piece of intact early-20th-century urban context, particularly alongside the royal bathing huts still standing on the beach.
